about: Beacon safety cards. Written for this hackathon demo in plain spoken English, following widely published public first-aid and preparedness guidance (American Red Cross, American Heart Association, CDC, Ready.gov, US Forest Service). NOT medically reviewed. The language model never writes steps; it only picks a card and answers questions from the card text.

cards.title: Severe bleeding
cards.summary: A wound is bleeding heavily and will not stop.
cards.call: Call emergency services as soon as you have any signal.

steps.text: Press hard directly on the wound with a clean cloth, a shirt, or your bare hand.
Keep firm, steady pressure for ten minutes. Do not lift the cloth to look.
If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and press harder. Leave the first layer in place.
If an arm or leg is still bleeding dangerously, put a tourniquet two to three inches above the wound, not over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops and note the time.
Keep the person lying down, warm and still until help arrives.

dont: Do not pull out an object stuck in the wound. Press around it instead.
Do not give food or drink.
redflags: Blood is spurting or pooling on the ground
The person is pale, cold, confused or faint
notes: A belt or a strip of cloth twisted tight with a stick can work as a tourniquet if nothing else is available.
cards.source: American Red Cross first aid, Stop the Bleed

cards.title: Not breathing: start CPR
cards.summary: Someone has collapsed, does not respond, and is not breathing normally.
cards.call: Send someone to call emergency services and to look for an AED right now.

steps.text: Tap the shoulders and shout. If there is no response and no normal breathing, start CPR now.
Send someone to call for help and find an AED. If you are alone, put your phone on speaker.
Kneel beside the chest. Put the heel of one hand on the center of the chest and your other hand on top.
Push hard and fast, about two inches deep, in time with the beat.
Let the chest rise fully between pushes. Never pause for more than ten seconds.
If you are trained, give two rescue breaths after every thirty pushes. If not, just keep pushing.
Keep going until the person breathes, an AED arrives, or someone takes over.

dont: Do not stop to check for a pulse over and over.
Do not be afraid of pushing too hard. Shallow pushes do not work.
redflags: Any adult who is unresponsive and not breathing normally needs CPR immediately
notes: For a child, use one or two hands and push about two inches deep.
For a baby, use two fingers or two thumbs and push about one and a half inches deep.
If an AED arrives, switch it on and follow its spoken instructions.

cards.title: Unconscious but breathing
cards.summary: Someone has passed out or cannot be woken, but is still breathing normally.
cards.call: Call emergency services, or send someone to find signal.

steps.text: Check breathing. Look, listen and feel for no more than ten seconds.
If they are breathing normally, roll them onto their side with the top knee bent and the head tilted slightly back.
Send someone for help, or call as soon as you have signal.
Keep them warm and watch their breathing the whole time.
If breathing stops or turns into gasping, roll them onto their back and start CPR.

dont: Do not give anything to eat or drink.
If you suspect a neck or back injury, move them only as much as needed to keep them breathing.
redflags: Breathing stops, or becomes noisy gasping
They hit their head, or do not wake within a minute

cards.title: Choking
cards.summary: Someone has food or an object stuck in their throat and cannot breathe or speak.
cards.call: If the blockage does not clear quickly, get someone to call emergency services.

steps.text: Ask, are you choking? If they can cough or speak, tell them to keep coughing hard.
If they cannot cough, speak or breathe, stand behind them and lean them forward.
Give five firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
Then give five abdominal thrusts. Make a fist just above the belly button, cover it with your other hand, and pull sharply in and up.
Keep repeating five back blows and five thrusts until the object comes out or they can breathe.
If the person becomes unresponsive, lower them to the ground and start CPR.

dont: Do not reach blindly into the mouth with your fingers.
Do not give water while they are choking.
redflags: Lips or face turning blue
The person goes limp or silent
notes: For a pregnant or very large person, give chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.
For a baby under one year, give five back blows and five chest thrusts. Never abdominal thrusts.

cards.title: Burns and scalds
cards.summary: Skin has been burned by fire, a hot surface, hot liquid or steam.
cards.call: Get medical help for large, deep, chemical or electrical burns.

steps.text: Get away from the heat. If clothing is on fire, stop, drop and roll.
Cool the burn under cool running water for at least ten minutes. Twenty is better.
Take off rings, watches and tight clothing near the burn before it swells. Leave anything that is stuck to the skin.
Cover the burn loosely with a clean non-stick dressing or clean plastic wrap.
Keep the person warm, and give small sips of water if they are fully alert.

dont: No ice, butter, oil or toothpaste on a burn.
Do not pop blisters.
redflags: The burn is bigger than the person's palm, or looks white, leathery or charred
The burn is on the face, hands, feet, genitals or over a joint
It is a chemical or electrical burn, or the person has trouble breathing
notes: If there is no running water, use any clean cool water, and keep pouring.

cards.title: Broken bone or bad sprain
cards.summary: A fall or twist has injured an arm, leg, ankle or wrist and it may be broken.
cards.call: Get help if the limb looks deformed, numb, cold or blue, or the bone is showing.

steps.text: Stop and take all weight off the injury. Do not try to straighten it.
If there is a wound, cover it with a clean cloth and press gently around it to control bleeding.
Splint it the way you found it. Pad a stick, a trekking pole or a rolled jacket, and tie it so the joints above and below cannot move.
Check the fingers or toes past the injury. They should be warm, pink and able to feel touch. Loosen the splint if they are not.
Hold something cold, wrapped in cloth, on the injury for up to twenty minutes, and raise the limb if that does not hurt more.
Rest, stay warm, and plan how to get help. Do not walk on a leg that cannot take weight.

dont: Do not push a bone back in.
Do not move someone with a possible neck or back injury unless they are in danger.
redflags: Bone is visible, or the limb is bent the wrong way
Fingers or toes are numb, cold or blue
The injury is to the head, neck, back or hip
notes: A sling for an arm can be made from a jacket or a shirt tied behind the neck.

cards.title: Hypothermia
cards.summary: Someone is dangerously cold: shivering hard, clumsy, confused or very sleepy.
cards.call: Hypothermia with confusion or drowsiness is an emergency. Get help as soon as you can.

steps.text: Get out of the wind, rain and snow, and put something between the person and the ground.
Gently swap wet clothes for dry layers. Cover the head and neck.
Wrap them in a sleeping bag, blankets or an emergency blanket. Share body heat if you need to.
Place warm, not hot, bottles or packs on the chest, neck and groin, wrapped in cloth.
If they are fully awake and can swallow, give warm sweet drinks and high-energy food.
Handle them gently, keep them lying flat, and keep warming until help arrives.

dont: No alcohol.
Do not rub the arms and legs, and do not use a hot bath.
redflags: Shivering stops but they are still cold
Confusion, slurred speech or extreme sleepiness
If they stop breathing, start CPR
cards.source: CDC, American Red Cross first aid

cards.title: Heat stroke and heat exhaustion
cards.summary: Someone is overheated: dizzy, sick, cramping, confused, or has collapsed in the heat.
cards.call: Confusion, fainting or hot dry skin means heat stroke. That is an emergency.

steps.text: Move to shade or a cool place and lie down. Stop all activity.
Take off extra clothing and gear.
Cool them fast. Soak the skin with water and fan hard, or sit them in cool water up to the neck if it is safe.
Put cold packs or wet cloths on the neck, armpits and groin.
If they are awake and not vomiting, give small sips of cool water or a sports drink.
Keep cooling until they feel better or help arrives.

dont: Do not give fever medicine such as aspirin or acetaminophen. It does not help.
Do not force fluids into someone who is confused or drowsy.
redflags: Confusion, fainting or a seizure
Skin is hot, and sweating has stopped
cards.source: CDC, American Red Cross first aid

cards.title: Snake bite
cards.summary: Someone has been bitten by a snake that may be venomous.
cards.call: Treat every snake bite as an emergency and get to medical care as fast as you safely can.

steps.text: Move away from the snake. Do not try to catch it or kill it.
Sit or lie down, and stay as calm and still as you can.
Take off rings, watches and tight clothing before swelling starts.
Wash the bite gently with soap and water if you have it, then cover it with a clean dry dressing.
Keep the bitten limb still in a comfortable position. Mark the edge of the swelling and write down the time.
Get to medical care. Walk slowly, and only if there is no other way out.

dont: Do not cut the bite or try to suck out venom.
No tourniquet and no ice.
No alcohol, caffeine, aspirin or ibuprofen.
redflags: Trouble breathing, drooping eyelids or slurred speech
Swelling that keeps spreading up the limb
notes: If it is safe, remember the snake's color and pattern, or take a photo from a distance.

cards.title: Severe allergic reaction
cards.summary: After a sting, food or medicine, someone has swelling, hives, wheezing or trouble breathing.
cards.call: Get emergency help even if they improve. The reaction can come back.

steps.text: If they carry an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now. Press it into the outer thigh and hold it for the time printed on the label.
Get emergency help as soon as you can, even if they start to feel better.
Lay them flat with their legs raised. If breathing is hard, let them sit up instead.
If they are not better after five to ten minutes, give a second auto-injector if there is one.
Stay with them and watch their breathing. If they stop breathing, start CPR.

dont: Do not make them stand up or walk.
Do not give food, drink or pills if they have trouble breathing or swallowing.
redflags: Trouble breathing, a tight throat or a hoarse voice
Swollen tongue or lips, or fainting
notes: The auto-injector can be used through clothing.

cards.title: Seizure
cards.summary: Someone is shaking or jerking and does not respond.
cards.call: Get emergency help if the seizure lasts more than five minutes or another one starts.

steps.text: Stay calm and note the time the seizure started.
Clear away anything hard or sharp. Ease them to the ground if they are standing.
Put something soft under the head and loosen anything tight around the neck.
Do not hold them down, and do not put anything in their mouth.
When the shaking stops, roll them onto their side and check they are breathing.
Stay with them and speak calmly until they are fully awake.

dont: Nothing in the mouth. They cannot swallow their tongue.
No food or water until they are fully alert.
redflags: The seizure lasts more than five minutes
They do not wake up or breathe normally afterwards
They are pregnant, diabetic, injured, or it happened in water

cards.title: Possible stroke
cards.summary: Sudden face drooping, arm weakness, strange speech or confusion.
cards.call: A stroke is an emergency. Get help by any means you have.

steps.text: Check the face. Ask them to smile. Does one side droop?
Check the arms. Ask them to raise both. Does one drift down?
Check speech. Ask them to repeat a simple sentence. Is it slurred or strange?
If you see any of these signs, treat it as an emergency and note the time the symptoms began.
Rest them on their side with the head slightly raised, and reassure them.
Get help by any means. Send someone to find signal, or travel to where you can call.

dont: No food, drink or medicine, including aspirin.
redflags: Any one of the face, arm or speech signs
Sudden severe headache, or loss of vision or balance
notes: Hospitals need to know when the person was last well. Write the time down.

cards.title: Lost with no signal
cards.summary: You have lost the trail or do not know where you are, and your phone has no service.
cards.call: Try an emergency call or text from high, open ground. Emergency calls can use any network in range.

steps.text: Stop walking. Sit down, breathe, and drink some water. Panic is the real danger.
Think. When did you last know exactly where you were? Do not move again until you have a plan.
Look around for trail markers, landmarks, the weather, and how much daylight is left.
If you are not sure of the way back, stay where you are. People who stay put are found sooner.
Make yourself easy to find. Put bright clothing in the open, and give three whistle blasts or shouts, again and again.
Before dark, put on all your layers and make a shelter from the wind and rain.
Save your phone. Use low power mode, dim the screen, and try an emergency call or text from high open ground.

dont: Do not split up the group.
Do not travel in the dark or follow a stream down steep ground.
redflags: Someone is injured, very cold or out of water
A storm or darkness is close
notes: Three of anything, such as whistle blasts, light flashes or fires, is the standard distress signal.
cards.source: US Forest Service, If You Get Lost

cards.title: Earthquake
cards.summary: The ground is shaking, or a strong earthquake has just happened.
cards.call: Text instead of calling so the network stays free for emergencies.

steps.text: Drop to your hands and knees right now.
Cover your head and neck. Get under a sturdy table or desk if one is close.
Hold on until the shaking stops. Stay away from windows and heavy furniture.
When it stops, check yourself and others for injuries, and put on sturdy shoes.
If you smell gas or see damage, get out and move to open ground. Use the stairs, never the elevator.
Expect aftershocks. Drop, cover and hold on each time.
If you are near the coast, move to high ground as soon as the shaking stops.

dont: Do not run outside while the ground is shaking.
Do not light matches or candles if there could be a gas leak.
redflags: Smell of gas, or sparks and damaged wiring
Cracks in walls or a leaning building
notes: If you are in bed, stay there and cover your head with a pillow.
If you are trapped, tap on a pipe or wall instead of shouting, to save air.

cards.title: Power outage
cards.summary: The electricity is out and you do not know for how long.
cards.call: Call for help if someone depends on powered medical equipment.

steps.text: Use flashlights or your phone light, not candles.
Keep the fridge and freezer closed. Food stays safe for about four hours in the fridge and forty-eight hours in a full freezer.
Unplug sensitive electronics and switch off appliances, so nothing surges when the power returns.
Stay warm or cool safely. Use layers and blankets in the cold, and shade, water and moving air in the heat.
Check on neighbors, older people, and anyone who relies on powered medical equipment.
Save your phone. Use low power mode, dim the screen, and keep one device switched off as a spare.

dont: Never run a generator, grill or camp stove indoors or in a garage. The fumes can kill.
Do not heat your home with a gas oven.
redflags: Headache, dizziness or nausea near a generator or stove means carbon monoxide. Get to fresh air.
Someone depends on powered medical equipment
notes: Leave one light switched on so you know when the power is back.

cards.title: Flood
cards.summary: Water is rising around you, or a flash flood warning has been given.
cards.call: If you are trapped by rising water, signal for help from the highest point you can reach.

steps.text: Move to higher ground or a higher floor now. Do not wait.
Never walk or drive through flood water. Six inches of moving water can knock you off your feet.
Turn off the electricity at the main breaker, but only if you can reach it from a dry spot.
Take water, medicines, your phone, a charger and warm clothes with you.
If you are trapped, go to the highest level. Go onto the roof only if you must, and signal for help.
Stay out of flood water afterwards. It can hide debris, sewage and live wires.

dont: Do not climb into a closed attic. You could be trapped by rising water.
Do not touch electrical equipment if you are wet or standing in water.
redflags: Water is moving fast or rising quickly
Downed power lines near water
